content: 1. There is no evidence to suggest that mebendazole, even when administered at high doses, is effective in treating hydatid disease. 2. Rare cases of neutropenia and agranulocytosis have been reported in patients who took mebendazole for prolonged periods and at dosages significantly higher than the recommended levels. 3. During extended therapy with mebendazole, it is advisable to periodically assess organ system functions, including hematopoietic and hepatic systems. 4. Patients should be informed about the potential risks to the fetus if mebendazole is taken during pregnancy, particularly during the first trimester. 5. Patients should also be advised that maintaining cleanliness is crucial to prevent reinfection and transmission of the infection. 6. In carcinogenicity studies conducted on mice and rats, no carcinogenic effects were observed at doses as high as 40 mg/kg (equivalent to one to two times the human dose based on mg/m²) administered daily over two years. 7. Dominant lethal mutation tests in mice showed no mutagenic effects at single doses as high as 640 mg/kg (18 times the human dose based on mg/m²). 8. Other tests, including the spermatocyte test, the F1 translocation test, and the Ames test, did not indicate any mutagenic properties of mebendazole. 9. Doses up to 40 mg/kg in mice (equivalent to the human dose based on mg/m²), administered to males for 60 days and to females for 14 days prior to gestation, had no adverse effects on fetuses or offspring, although slight maternal toxicity was observed. 10. Mebendazole has demonstrated embryotoxic and teratogenic effects in pregnant rats at single oral doses as low as 10 mg/kg (approximately equivalent to the human dose based on mg/m²). 11. Based on these findings, the use of mebendazole is not recommended in pregnant women. 12. Although there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, a postmarketing survey of a limited number of women who inadvertently consumed mebendazole during the first trimester of pregnancy found that the incidence of spontaneous abortion and malformation did not exceed that of the general population. 13. Among 170 term deliveries, no teratogenic risk associated with mebendazole was identified. 14. It is not known whether mebendazole is excreted in human breast milk. Since many drugs are excreted in human milk, caution should be exercised when administering mebendazole to nursing women. 15. Mebendazole has not been extensively studied in children under two years of age. Therefore, when treating children under two years, the relative benefit-to-risk ratio should be carefully considered.
